title: Gaze modeling in multi-party dialogues and extraversion expression through gaze aversion control

fields.value: Technical/system-description study with two video-based subjective experiments.

quotes.text: In this study, we developed a gaze motion generation model, focusing on three features: (1) the gaze target (towards dialogue partners or gaze aversion), (2) the gaze duration, and (3) the eyeball direction during gaze aversion.

In this user study, we used the gaze model parameters of the two individuals Person A and Person B (PA and PB) described in the previous sections and conducted video-based experiments to compare the impressions on the gaze behaviors generated by each of the models (PA-M and PB-M).

By considering that gaze aversion is a crucial factor for expressing extraversion, in this user study, we conduct another video-based experiment to investigate the effects of explicitly controlling the gaze aversion ratio (GAR).

fields.value: Video-based, remote/online crowdsourced evaluation; participants watched videos rather than interacting directly with the robot. The paper does not name a physical study venue.

quotes.text: In this experiment, a total of 55 participants (27 males, 28 females) with an average age of 38.8 years (standard deviation of 10.7 years) were recruited using crowdsourcing services.

fields.value: Participants watched videos of an android robot in a three-party dialogue scenario with two humans and rated perceived robot extraversion and behavioral naturalness. Study 1 used seven videos; Study 2 used eight. Video clips were about 40 seconds each.

quotes.text: Video clips were created for each motion type, by recording the generated motions from the viewpoint of one of the dialogue partners on the right side of the robot and adding characters representing the dialogue partners on the left and bottom sides of the video.
Each video is about 40 s long, and it takes about 15 to 30 min to complete the task.
Each participant is required to view a total of eight videos.

After watching each video, participants were asked to rate their impressions of the robot’s personality on a 7-point scale (1: very introverted, 4: neutral, 7: very extraverted). The naturalness (human-likeness) of the robot’s behaviors was also rated on a 7-point scale (1: very unnatural, 4: neutral, 7: very natural).

fields.value: Three participants per dialogue scenario: one robot and two humans.

quotes.text: Video-based experiments have been conducted where participants watched videos of the robot talking with two humans, replicating the three-party dialogue scenarios used in this study.

For evaluating the gaze model, we adopted the android Nikola, which has a human-like appearance and human-like degrees of freedom for the eyeballs, eyelids, and head movements, which are important for gazing expressions.

fields.value: Seven-point subjective ratings of extraversion and behavioral naturalness; statistical comparisons used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni-adjusted p-values. Generated gaze aversion ratios were also measured in Study 1. The source dialogue dataset used manual annotations of dialogue roles, turn-taking, gaze events, and gaze targets.

Therefore, for multiple comparisons, we performed Wilcoxon’s signed-rank test with a significance level of 0.05 for each pair of models and corrected the p-values using the Bonferroni method.
To verify this, we measured the gaze aversion rates of the generated motions for PB voice and confirmed that the gaze aversion ratios were around 22% for PA-M, 36% for PB-M, and 56% for PB-R.
For the dialogue sessions including either one of the two target individuals, turn-taking, dialogue roles, gaze events, and gaze targets were annotated.

fields.value: In Study 1, for Person A’s voice, PB-M elicited lower extraversion ratings than PA-R and PA-M (Bonferroni-adjusted p = 0.0058 and 0.0059). For Person B’s voice, no significant differences were found. In Study 2, 20% versus 80% gaze aversion produced significantly different extraversion ratings for both voices (about 0.7–0.8 points); naturalness averages were 4–5 across conditions.

quotes.text: As shown in Figure 11(a), significant differences were found between PA-R/PB-M (W(N 27) 43.0, p 0.0058 0.01) and PA-M/PB-M (W(N 27) 27.5.0, p 0.0059 0.01), for Person A’s voice.

On the other hand, as shown in Figure 11(b), significant differences were found only between PB-R/PA-M (W(N 27) 83.5, p 0.095 0.1), for Person B’s voice. No significant differences could be found between PA-M/PB-M, contrary to our expectations.
Differences of around 0.7 to 0.8 points were found between the 20-M and 80-M conditions.

Specifically, a significant difference in extraversion was observed between the model with 80% gaze aversion and the model with 20% gaze towards the conversational partner (Person A voice; W(N 55) 58.5, p 0.008 0.01, Person B voice; W(N 55) 21.0, p 0.0001 0.001), regardless of the speaker.

fields.value: The paper frames its topic as gaze control/modeling for multi-party dialogue, covering partner-directed gaze and gaze aversion. It treats gaze as a nonverbal behavior related to dialogue facilitation, turn-taking, and personality expression.

quotes.text: Gaze control plays a crucial role in the context of conversational robots involving multiple participants.
The proposed model is described by three parameters, (1) the gaze target (towards dialogue partners or gaze aversion), (2) the gaze duration, and (3) the eyeball direction during gaze aversion.
In dialogue interactions, nonverbal information such as gestures, facial expressions, prosody, and gaze play important roles in facilitating interactions, in addition to linguistic information.

fields.value: The paper describes gaze as providing feedback, communicating emotional information, regulating dialogue flow, conveying turn-taking cues, and expressing personality. Its model selects gaze targets based on dialogue roles and turn-taking state.

quotes.text: Eye gaze has several essential functions in facilitating dialogue such as: providing feedback, communicating emotional information, and regulating dialogue flow.
Gaze is known to convey important functions related to turn-taking [7], as well as being strongly related to the expression of emotions and intentions [8–10].
A dialogue state understanding module is necessary since the gaze generation model requires information about dialogue roles and turn-taking states.

fields.value: In video ratings, more gaze aversion was associated with lower perceived extraversion: the 80% aversion model scored significantly differently from the 20% aversion model for either speaker’s voice. The authors report that gaze model choice also changed extraversion impressions, although the Study 1 effect was not found for Person B’s voice. Naturalness ratings were slightly positive across models.

quotes.text: From the results of this experiment, it was possible to demonstrate the hypothesis that ‘the model that averts gaze more has higher extraversion regardless of the speaker.’

Regarding the robot’s behavior naturalness, average scores between 4 and 5 were obtained for all videos, indicating that slightly natural behaviors could be generated by the gaze system, regardless of the gaze aversion ratio value.

Through subjective experiments, it was shown that the impression of extraversion levels changed when the robot’s gaze behaviors were controlled using different gaze generation models for the same speaker’s utterances.

fields.value: The system uses dialogue roles and turn-taking states, then samples a gaze target, duration, and gaze-aversion eye direction from speaker-derived model parameters. Robot motion control uses look/look-away commands for eye and head movement, limits head speed, and inserts a blink for large direction changes. Dialogue roles and turns were manually annotated for this study’s analysis.

quotes.text: In this study, the following three roles are considered: role ∈{Speaker, Addressee, SideParticipant}

First, a random value p (0 ≤p ≤1) is extracted from a uniform distribution. Then, the Gaze Target is determined based on p and the gazing ratios described by S for Speaker, Addressee, Side Participant, and Gaze Aversion.

The gaze aversion pattern is generated by sampling from the distributions obtained from the data for the first and second aversions, and moving back to the first and second positions alternately if the eyeballs move three or more times within a gaze aversion event.

Two types of commands are prepared: one is a ‘look’ function to move the eyeballs and head orientation to look at a specific point, while the other is a ‘look away’ function to move the eyeballs to a specified direction to deal with gaze aversion.

fields.value: The robot platform was Nikola, an android with a human-like appearance, 32 facial degrees of freedom and 3 neck degrees of freedom; gaze control used the eyeballs, eyelids, and head.

quotes.text: For evaluating the gaze model, we adopted the android Nikola, which has a human-like appearance and human-like degrees of freedom for the eyeballs, eyelids, and head movements, which are important for gazing expressions.
Nikola has 32 degrees of freedoms (DOFs) for the face and 3 DOFs for the neck and can express human-like facial expressions [31], as well as human-like gaze behaviors.

fields.value: The authors selected an android with human-like eye, eyelid, and head degrees of freedom because these movements were considered important for gaze expression. They also state that eye movement, in addition to head movement, can make gaze aversion more natural and human-like.

quotes.text: For evaluating the gaze model, we adopted the android Nikola, which has a human-like appearance and human-like degrees of freedom for the eyeballs, eyelids, and head movements, which are important for gazing expressions.
In our previous study, it was shown that robots can express more natural human-like behaviors by moving the eyeballs, than by moving only the head, to avert the gaze.
These short gaze aversions, which are made by moving the eyeballs, are thought to be important to increase the human-likeness of the robot’s motions.

fields.value: The authors built a gaze-generation model for a robot in three-party dialogue, based on gaze patterns from two people with different extraversion scores. In video evaluations, changing gaze aversion ratios changed perceived extraversion for both dialogue voices; naturalness ratings were slightly positive across conditions.

RQ1; RQ2; RQ3; RQ4; RQ5; RQ6 — The paper relates gaze to dialogue regulation, turn-taking, feedback, and personality, models gaze behavior using dialogue roles and gaze-aversion parameters, and evaluates perceived extraversion and naturalness with an android. It also discusses how eye and head movement capabilities informed the choice and implementation of the robot embodiment.
